extracted.intended_audience: fiction and nonfiction narrative writers; writing students, teachers, and writing-group members
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes three of Ursula K. Le Guin's craft-focused exercises (sound of prose, economizing modifiers, and invisible exposition) with explanations, examples, anti-patterns, and practice prompts for narrative writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice hearing the sound of your writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Refine the sound (music, rhythm, timing) of your prose so it reads well silently or aloud; avoid dull, choppy, droning, jerky, feeble narrative and aim for lively, well-paced, flowing, strong, beautiful prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Le Guin: “Dull, choppy, droning, jerky, feeble: these common criticisms of narrative are all faults in the sound of it. Lively, well-paced, flowing, strong, beautiful: these are all qualities of the sound of prose...” Advice emphasizes placement and timing of words, sentence-rhythm changes to express emotion, and even character/place names contributing to beauty. Example/guidance from Gary Provost demonstrates varying sentence length to create musicality (short, medium, occasional long 'crescendo' sentences). Exercise (verbatim prompt): "Write a paragraph to a page of narrative that’s meant to be read aloud. Use onomatopoeia, alliteration, rhythmic effects, made-up words or names, dialect — any kind of sound effect you like — but not rhyme or meter." The post notes this is a playful warm-up and recommends reading aloud or imagining oral delivery to test sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice eliminating unnecessary adjectives and adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid lazy or overused adjectives and adverbs that bloat prose; prefer putting qualities into verbs or nouns (they ran quickly → they raced; a growling voice → a growl); watch for words rendered meaningless by overuse (e.g., 'great', 'suddenly', 'somehow') and weasel qualifiers ('kind of', 'just').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Le Guin: “Adjectives and adverbs are rich and good and nourishing…They cause obesity in prose only when used lazily or overused. When the quality that the adverb indicates can be put in the verb itself... the prose will be cleaner, more intense, more vivid…Some adjectives and adverbs have become meaningless through literary overuse.” Anti-patterns listed: redundant modifiers ("white snow"), filler/weasel words ("somehow", "kind of", "just"), and overused words that lose weight ("great"). Exercise (verbatim prompt): "Write a paragraph to a page (200–350 words) of descriptive narrative prose without adjectives or adverbs. No dialogue. The point is to give a vivid description of a scene or an action using only verbs, nouns, pronouns, and articles. Adverbs of time (then, next, later, etc) may be necessary, but be sparing." The post notes this trains specificity and intensifies imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice strengthening invisible exposition (avoid expository lumps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Convey background information subtly so it doesn't read as a lecture or 'Expository Lump'; break exposition into small, integral details that build the story ("grind it fine, and make it into bricks") and never allow info-dumps that jar narrative pace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Le Guin warns against characters lecturing to deliver information (example: "Oh, Captain, do tell me how the anti-matter dissimulator works!") and describes the goal as making exposition 'invisible.' The post reproduces several exercise parts to practice this skill: 1) Dialogue-only characterization: "Tell a story and present two characters through dialogue alone. Write it like a play, with A and B as the characters’ names. No stage directions. No description of the characters." Guidance: don't have characters say things they'd never say in real life; work information in naturally (example dialogue provided). 2) Describe a character via place: "Describe a character by describing any place inhabited or frequented by that character…Give us evidences that build up into a consistent, coherent mood or atmosphere, from which we can infer…the absent person…A mere inventory of articles won’t do it... Every detail must tell." Guidance: no action or people in this exercise—the 'stage without the actors.' 3) Scene-with-process exercise: "Think of something you know how to do that involves a complex series of specific actions...Write a scene, involving at least two people, in which this process is going on, either in the background of a conversation or as the locus of the action. Keep the description specific and concrete." Guidance: avoid turning this into an info-dump; keep exposition integrated into action or dialogue so it remains invisible. The post notes these exercises are especially useful for genres (like SF/F) with lots of unfamiliar information but apply to any narrative writing.
